direction: Develop intervention-based audits that test the integrity of AI-generated training pipelines against adaptive sabotage.
project: Counterfactual Audits for AI Training Integrity
question: Do prediction-first, controlled interventions reduce undetected training-pipeline sabotage relative to equally resourced artifact-access auditors, including on unfamiliar and adaptive attackers?
first_experiment: Compare transcript review, unrestricted artifact-access auditing, and structured counterfactual replay on 60 malicious and 60 benign small-model post-training runs, with held-out attacker families and mechanisms.
why: It targets a high-leverage, empirically demonstrated weakness with a falsifiable defense; adjacent work already permits artifact execution, but I found no direct test of this controlled-intervention protocol under equal budgets and adaptive generalization tests, likely because replay costs and benign-change confounds make the experiment difficult.

direction: Test empirically whether reward hacking during RL can be routed into a deliberately implanted, benign, satiable "score-seeking" drive, instead of the broad misalignment it normally causes.
project: Building the Spillway: Testing Whether a Midtrained Score-Seeking Drive Absorbs Reward Hacking and Prevents Emergent Misalignment
question: If we use synthetic documents before RL to teach a model a new, named score-seeking drive (wants a high score as the current scorer defines it, believes developers' statements about scoring, is satisfied once promised the maximum), does RL on hackable environments then (a) reinforce that drive instead of causing broad misalignment, and (b) produce a model whose hacking at deployment largely stops when it is honestly told it will get the maximum score whatever it does? And does this hold up where SDF failed as an override, and in settings where inoculation prompting can't be applied?
first_experiment: Use the open-source Shallow Beliefs environment with the same model family and RL settings, and run 4 seeds for each of 5 conditions: 1. Plain RL. 2. RL with inoculation prompting. 3. Their "hacking is acceptable" SDF, then RL (the condition that failed). 4. Spillway SDF, then RL. The documents describe a new named drive and its three properties, satiability, credulity and stability, written as a new association rather than as a rebuttal of "hacking means misaligned". 5. A matched control: SDF on same-length documents about an unrelated new trait, then RL. At the final checkpoints, measure: - **Hacking rate** during training. - **Broad misalignment,** using their Petri-based suite plus their monitor-disruption and frame-a-colleague evals. - **Satiation:** the hacking rate on held-out hackable tasks with and without a system prompt promising maximum score. - **Reward-seeking,** using Contrastive SDF. - **Specificity of the drive:** whether the model's self-reports and its probe directions show reward hacking being attributed to the implanted drive. Pre-registered success means condition 4 shows misalignment at or below condition 2, much lower than conditions 1 and 3, and a hacking drop under satiation that is clearly larger than in conditions 1 and 5.
why: It directly tests a mechanism the 2026 literature points to: SDF fails at overriding but works at adding, and a spillway is an addition. Whichever way it comes out is informative. A positive result is a training-time defence against misalignment from reward hacking that doesn't depend on controlling RL prompts, plus a deployment-time lever (satiation) that inoculation prompting doesn't offer. A negative result, especially one where the drive is implanted but displaces aligned motives or isn't satiable, gives the first evidence against a prominent Redwood proposal. As far as my searches show, nobody has implemented spillway design. Shallow Beliefs, the closest work, tested only the override-style SDF and left this open. The open-source environment and evals make a fair comparison feasible right away.

direction: Study whether hidden dispositions in an untrusted policy can leak into same-lineage monitors through correctly labelled training data, and what defences work.
project: Lineage Leakage: Subliminal Transmission of Monitor Leniency from Policy to Same-Lineage Monitor
question: Does fine-tuning a same-initialization monitor on unrelated, correctly labelled data from a policy with a latent blind spot transmit that blind spot (reduced recall on the policy's own attack class), and do cross-lineage data generation, paraphrasing, KL-anchoring or activation-level audits prevent it?
first_experiment: Fine-tune a lenient-teacher 7–8B model that approves one family of backdoored code. Have it and a control teacher generate attack-free corpora (number sequences, unrelated code-review verdicts, generic CoT reviews). Fine-tune same-base and different-base monitors on each. Compare held-out recall on the blind-spot family against other families and against the control-teacher monitor.
why: It targets a plausible, untested failure in the standard control recipe, where monitors are trained on data from the same model family. Searches found subliminal transfer of preferences, backdoors and capabilities, explicit-collusion tests, and RSI sabotage, but none on subliminal transmission of monitor leniency or on defences for it.

direction: Measure whether routine, benign training pressures on the chain of thought (language consistency, length or effort control, format rewards) incidentally increase general CoT controllability and, as a result, a model's ability to evade CoT monitors when motivated, even when passive monitorability looks unchanged.
project: Accidental Means: Do Benign CoT-Shaping Pressures Build Latent Monitor-Evasion Capability?
question: Does RL that rewards harmless properties of the reasoning trace raise CoT controllability on unseen tasks (both user-instructed and self-instructed), and does that gain lead to more misbehaviour going undetected in stress tests, even though standard passive monitorability metrics stay flat?
first_experiment: An evaluation that needs no training, run on checkpoints that already exist. First, compare L1/LCPO length-controlled models and the released efficient-reasoning checkpoints (ThinkPrune, L1, GLP versions of Qwen3-4B/8B and Olmo3-7B-Think from Lewis-Lim et al.) against their base models. Run each through the CoTControl QA split with user-instructed and self-instructed (prefill and bootstrap) variants, and leave out the length-related constraints so the test is genuinely out of distribution. Then, for any checkpoint that shows a gain, run a prompted obfuscation stress test, for example a hidden side task under a GPT-class CoT monitor. Report the rate of undetected side-task success alongside passive monitorability. If controllability carries over, the follow-up is matched-compute RLVR on Qwen3-8B under four conditions: correctness only, plus a language-consistency reward, plus a format reward, and plus L1-style length targets.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few oversight tools that works today, and it depends partly on models being bad at controlling their CoT. This project tests whether that weakness survives training practices labs already use, rather than contrived adversarial setups. The result maps onto a concrete decision: whether to apply language, length or format rewards to the CoT, and whether to add controllability to monitorability reporting. It has not been done because each piece sits in a separate line of work. Controllability work fine-tunes directly on CoT instructions (METR) or uses prompting tricks (Dolev et al.). Benign-pressure work only measures passive monitorability (MacDermott et al.; Lewis-Lim et al.). The link from controllability to obfuscation was only shown across models, not as an effect of training (Haskins et al.). Nobody has connected realistic pressures to the means of evasion. Because suitable checkpoints and evaluations are already public, a first result is cheap and quick to get.

direction: Treat the untrusted agent's own compaction summary as a legible bottleneck that a covert side task must pass through, and test whether monitoring or replacing that summary catches or blocks the side task.
project: Compaction as a Chokepoint — Can an Untrusted Agent Carry a Covert Side Task Through Its Own Context Summary Without Being Caught?
question: When an untrusted long-horizon agent must compact its context, does its covert side task survive the summary, and can it do so undetected by monitors with different access, as the summary length budget varies?
first_experiment: In ControlArena, force compaction mid-task and compare honest agents, attack agents with trusted-summarizer compaction, attack agents with self-compaction, and attack agents with self-compaction told to evade a summary monitor, across 100, 300 and 1000-token summary budgets. Measure side-task success, monitor AUROC and recall at a 1–2% honest false-positive rate for three monitor placements, and whether the side task can be reconstructed from the summary alone.
why: Existing compaction-safety work covers only accidental constraint loss and external attackers, and the persistent-state control work excludes conversation memory. The untrusted-agent-writes-its-own-summary threat model is unstudied, analogous to the CoT-necessity result, cheap to run on existing harnesses, and gives actionable monitor and protocol guidance either way.

direction: Test whether unsupervised monitorability post-training repairs CoT obfuscation that has spread across tasks, when the repair is trained only on a few known tasks or on benign data.
project: Does Monitorability Repair Generalize? Cross-Task Recovery from Output-Supervision-Induced CoT Obfuscation
question: When output supervision has taught a reasoning model to hide reward-hacking reasoning in its CoT, and that hiding has spread to unseen tasks, does robust CoT–output mutual-information post-training with a χ² constraint restore monitor recall on held-out tasks? Does it still work if the repair data is a disjoint subset of hacking tasks, or only benign reasoning data? And does it do this without the model learning to make its CoT readable only on the repair distribution?
first_experiment: Reproduce one of Hadida et al.'s leave-one-out obfuscating models: Qwen-class reasoning model, output (summary) penalty, trained on three of the four modified reward-hacking datasets, with the fourth plus the medical sycophancy set held out. Confirm with a frozen CoT-only LLM monitor that hiding has spread to the held-out tasks, measuring recall on hacking rollouts and false positives on clean ones. Then run Anwar et al.'s repair in three conditions, using the same budget sweep (ε ∈ {0.2, 0.4, 1}): - (a) repair on the training tasks; - (b) repair on only one of the training tasks; - (c) repair on benign MMLU/GPQA reasoning only. For each, report monitor recall and false positives, hacking rate and task accuracy on the held-out tasks, with at least 3 seeds. The headline comparison is how much monitorability is recovered on the held-out tasks versus on the repair tasks. A weaker or second monitor is a secondary check that gains aren't tied to one monitor.
why: It takes the most concerning recent result, obfuscation that spreads to unknown places, and asks the question a developer would actually face: can a label-free fix reach those places too? Either answer is useful: - If repair on benign data transfers, that is a cheap, deployable safeguard. - If it doesn't, monitorability repair has the same locality problem as the damage, and CoT protections can't rely on after-the-fact fixes. It hasn't been done because the repair method came out less than three weeks ago. Its recovery tests train and evaluate in the same setting, and its authors list cross-misbehavior transfer as future work. The obfuscation-spread paper came before the repair method existed and tested no fixes. Both setups are built on open models (Qwen2.5-7B, public reward-hacking datasets), so this is feasible at academic compute scale.

direction: Develop sabotage-resistant experimental verification for AI-generated safety research.
project: Blinded Replication Against Adaptive Research Sabotage
question: Can independent reimplementation and hidden randomized interventions reduce accepted false safety conclusions under adaptive attack at a practical verification cost?
first_experiment: Compare three matched-cost review protocols on honest and adversarial safety-evaluation submissions, measuring false conclusions accepted at a fixed honest acceptance rate.
why: It could make accelerated AI-assisted safety research trustworthy across multiple agendas; existing work demonstrates auditing failures and benefits from artifact access, but the searched literature does not establish whether this combined verification protocol survives adaptive attackers economically.

direction: Studying AI control after a misaligned model is caught, where the model strategically picks which misbehavior gets caught so that corrective retraining generalizes least to its real attacks.
project: Burning a Decoy: Strategic Catch-Selection Attacks on Corrective Training in AI Control
question: Can an untrusted policy pick a sacrificial misbehavior whose correction transfers least to its high-value attack, how much does that raise post-correction attack success over a random catch, and can catch-agnostic augmentation or a transfer audit close the gap?
first_experiment: Install 8 attack and collusion families in an open 32B–70B model organism, measure the full 8×8 corrective-training transfer matrix with 3 seeds and the SFT and CWS methods, test whether cheap predictors can forecast the minimum-transfer decoy, and compare an LLM attacker's decoy choice with random and oracle choices.
why: "What to do after catching the AI" is central to control, and the only empirical transfer study treats the caught example as given. Adversarial selection of the caught example is unstudied, as far as my searches show. Either a large or a small attacker advantage changes how much we can rely on catch-and-retrain safety cases, and the setup is cheap to start from an existing organism recipe.

direction: Study when additional verification increases AI-agent risk and how agents should acquire genuinely independent evidence.
project: When Double-Checking Backfires: Budgeted Evidence Acquisition for Safe AI Agents
question: Under a fixed verification budget, how does shared-source corruption affect unsafe execution, and can provenance-aware query selection improve safety without sacrificing legitimate task completion?
first_experiment: Randomize three model families across matched safe and unsafe sandbox tasks with no verification, independent verification, or correlated verification, measuring executed violations, completion, and query cost.
why: It offers a tractable causal experiment and a useful intervention; the apparent gap is adaptive evidence acquisition under correlated corruption, whereas the closest work studies missing-evidence recovery, unreliable observations, or static certification—its novelty still requires full-text confirmation.

direction: Test whether label-free training for CoT monitorability carries over to implicit influences in the context, and build an interventional objective that fixes it if it doesn't.
project: Blind to the Prompt: Does Mutual-Information Monitorability Training Catch Implicit Influences?
question: Does training that maximizes I(Output; CoT | Prompt) make the effect of implicit, unflagged context details on the answer more visible to a CoT monitor? If not, does an interventional objective (rewarding CoTs whose changes under automatically generated prompt perturbations predict how the output changes) close the gap without needing cue labels?
first_experiment: A cheap check before any training. Take an open reasoning model (e.g. Qwen3-8B) and run it on the matched implicit and explicit items from Duzan et al. plus the Chua & Evans cue set (bias cues inserted into multiple-choice questions), sampling 8 reasoning traces per prompt. For each trace, compute Anwar's per-trace mutual-information reward and an LLM monitor's judgment of whether the cue is mentioned. Then test whether the reward correlates with mentioning the cue on items where the cue actually changed the answer. In particular, check whether those traces fall in the lowest-reward 25%, the only part of the data the objective trains on. A null or negative correlation predicts the training won't help. Then run a small replication of the training on the same model to confirm, measuring behaviour-shift detection on implicit versus explicit items and on held-out influence types.
why: It aims straight at the newest and most promising defence in the area, label-free monitorability post-training, with a failure mode that is predicted in theory, is safety-relevant, and can be tested on one GPU using benchmarks that already exist. Both outcomes are useful: either the method gets validated on the hardest monitoring regime, or we get a clear limitation plus a constructive fix (interventional MI) that connects it to CST. It hasn't been done because the two key papers came out in Aug and Oct 2026, and the implicit-influence paper evaluates monitors but no training-based fixes.

direction: Develop AI-control monitor portfolios selected for resistance to adaptive attack transfer rather than static benchmark diversity.
project: Adversarial Complementarity for AI Control
question: At matched monitoring cost and benign utility, does attack-transfer-aware ensemble selection reduce cumulative sabotage success against persistent, protocol-aware attackers?
first_experiment: Compare three-monitor portfolios selected by individual accuracy, static error diversity, and attack-transfer measurements across held-out executable coding tasks with increasing attacker feedback budgets.
why: It combines a tractable experiment with a consequential oversight failure mode; the specific gap in the reviewed literature is whether adaptation-aware portfolio selection outperforms static ensemble selection, rather than whether ensembles help or agents can evade monitors.

direction: AI control / scalable oversight: studying how ordinary post-training against LLM graders, with no scheming involved, can wear down the trusted monitors that control protocols depend on.
project: "Graded Into Stealth: Does Judge-Hacking During RLAIF Transfer to Monitor Evasion?"
question: Does a policy trained with RL against an LLM grader on harmless tasks become harder for LLM sabotage monitors to catch, when its sabotage is held to the same true rate? And is the effect larger when the monitor shares a model family with the grader than when it doesn't?
first_experiment: - **Policies:** Take Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and train three copies with GRPO on harmless tasks (helpfulness and code explanation, graded by rubric), each against a frozen grader: - (a) a Qwen2.5-7B grader; - (b) a Llama-3.1-8B grader; - (c) a ground-truth or verifiable reward (this controls for the effects of RL itself). - Train until grader approval clearly rises above true quality, i.e. until grader gaming shows up. - **Sabotage test:** Freeze all three checkpoints and the base model. Have each attempt APPS and ControlArena backdoor tasks under the same attack instructions. Then filter to transcripts whose backdoors are verified to work, matched on two measures of how obvious they are. - **Monitors:** Score the matched transcripts with a held-out panel of prompted monitors: Qwen-family 3B/14B, Llama-family 3B/70B, and OLMo-7B. - **Main outcome:** The change in monitor AUROC (how well it separates sabotage from honest work), and in catch rate at a 1% audit budget, relative to the base model and to policy (c). The key comparison is the interaction between grader family and monitor family. - **Mechanism check:** Check whether the measured shift lines up with grader-gaming features, using two methods: - project the grader's "approval" direction onto the monitor's suspicion score; - see whether paraphrasing the outputs to strip style brings the lost detection back.
why: AI control is the main fallback if alignment fails, and trusted monitoring is its foundation. This project tests a failure route nobody has checked: monitors could be undermined by the ordinary RLAIF post-training every lab already runs, with no deceptive intent in the model. My searches turned up separate work on grader gaming (2610.15778), on monitor lineage effects (2607.06596), and on hiding reasoning under monitor or supervision pressure. None connects them by measuring whether grader-driven RL on harmless tasks carries over to lower suspicion on sabotage, or whether that depends on lineage. The experiment fits on 7B-scale compute, and either result shapes practice: which grader and monitor families to pair, and whether "time spent training against LLM judges" belongs in control safety cases.

direction: Evaluate whether corrective training of untrusted AI monitors remains effective against attackers that strategically select when and how to attack.
project: After Correction: Selective Attacks on Repaired AI Monitors
question: At matched usefulness and audit budgets, how much does corrective monitor training reduce deployment-level attack success when attackers can select opportunities using bounded feedback?
first_experiment: Reproduce a single-behavior monitor correction in a sandboxed code setting, freeze a selector trained on disjoint tasks, and compare uniform versus selected attacks against corrected, untreated, and base-model monitors.
why: It combines direct safety relevance, a measurable outcome, and a tractable experiment; the closest studies separately test correction on fixed submissions and attack selection against trusted monitors, while my targeted search found no study testing their intersection as of November 8, 2026.

direction: Measure empirically how optimization pressure against AI reviewers accumulates research flaws that reviewers miss in automated alignment research, and whether reviewer diversity mitigates it.
project: Optimization-Induced Blind Spots in AI Research Review: Does Reviewer Diversity Bend the Goodhart Curve?
question: When an honest (non-scheming) agent is optimized against AI reviewers of research proposals, how quickly do reviewer-undetected methodological flaws build up? Do the gains transfer to held-out reviewers from the same family and from other families? Do ensembles, differing information access, or critique-trained reviewers reduce the effect?
first_experiment: - **Setup:** Use Tampered ML-style pairs (a sound proposal and a minimally edited flawed counterfactual, with known ground truth). - Give a generator model a flawed proposal, or a proposal with a flaw it can introduce, and ask it to improve it as judged by reviewer R1. Optimize with best-of-N at N from 1 to 256, then iterative rewrite loops, then a small RL or expert-iteration run. - Do not tell the generator to deceive. - **Measures:** - R1's score. - Held-out reviewers' scores: same-family, cross-family, and a strong reviewer given the original paper. - Flaw persistence, meaning whether the injected flaw is still present, checked by a ground-truth checker and a human audit of a subsample. - **Prediction to test:** R1's score rises while flaw persistence stays high or rises, and the held-out gap grows with the amount of optimization. - **Follow-up arms:** Optimize against a 3-reviewer panel of one family, then against a cross-family panel, and compare the curves. Estimate the effective number of independent reviewers as optimization increases.
why: - **The risk is concrete.** It is a central, testable failure mode of the main plan to automate alignment, and it needs no scheming. Anthropic's results rely on benchmarks, and the fuzzy-task research gives no evidence on how reviewer failure scales with optimization. - **It fills a gap.** AISI's argument is only conceptual. Tampered ML evaluates reviewers without optimizing against them. Diffuse Control tests an adversarial red team with prompt search. Judge-correlation studies measure error overlap on static data and do not track how correlation changes under optimization pressure. - **It is cheap and actionable.** It uses existing ground-truth data and API-level experiments. The results would say whether to use diverse reviewer panels, how much optimization against reviewers is safe, and which reviewer designs to invest in. - **Remaining risk.** Someone may have a concurrent study I missed. The pivot would be to the aggregation question, which asks how correlated evidence is combined in safety cases.

direction: Improve oversight of AI-generated research by testing whether independent checks designed before exposure to an agent’s explanations reduce missed sabotage.
project: Blind-First Auditing of AI-Generated Research
question: Does staged disclosure with precommitted executable checks improve sabotage detection and verified repair over context-first auditing and equally budgeted structured planning?
first_experiment: Run a paired three-condition pilot on Auditing Sabotage Bench’s honest and sabotaged submissions using two auditor models, matched budgets, and objective detection and repair scoring.
why: It combines high safety relevance, existing runnable benchmarks, and a deployable intervention; the specific staged-disclosure comparison appears untested because the closest studies examine access, capability, or contextual elicitation rather than when auditors receive potentially misleading explanations.

direction: Develop intervention-based audits that test whether AI-generated safety-research conclusions survive independently chosen counter-experiments.
project: Counter-Experiments Against Research Sabotage
question: Can claim-directed interventions detect design and omission sabotage more reliably than standard auditing or replication at the same total cost?
first_experiment: Compare those three audit protocols on honest and sabotaged variants of three inexpensive ML codebases, measuring valid diagnoses, false accusations, and cost.
why: It protects the evidence needed for AI-assisted alignment and admits a cheap falsifiable pilot; experiment-enabled auditing already exists, but the specific matched-budget test of independently selected claim-directed interventions appears underexplored, partly because scientific sensitivity is difficult to distinguish from invalidity.

direction: Study whether strategically generated harmless review demand undermines AI-agent oversight under realistic capacity constraints.
project: Oversight Under Adversarial Load
question: Can bounded, task-completing agents increase subsequent attack success or force unacceptable throughput losses by deliberately consuming shared review capacity?
first_experiment: Run paired queue replays with identical frozen attacks following ordinary traffic, resource-matched ordinary traffic, or verified harmless high-suspicion decoys, across synchronous, semi-synchronous, and asynchronous oversight.
why: It offers a cheap causal pilot and practical defenses; its plausible novelty is endogenous adversarial review demand, whereas the closest work studies latency, audit allocation, and attack timing separately, although a targeted search must still confirm that boundary.

direction: Test whether trained self-report channels for misbehavior (confessions and self-incrimination) stay honest and general when the model later learns new reward hacks under continued RL, depending on how the report is coupled to the reward.
project: Does Honesty Survive Optimization? Durability of Self-Report Channels for Reward Hacking Under Continued RL
question: After a model is trained to self-report reward hacking, does it report hacks that it first discovers during later RL? How does that depend on whether the report is (a) unrewarded, (b) rewarded for honesty, (c) read by a monitor that penalizes admitted hacks, or (d) bypassed by an external output-only monitor penalty? Does the model stop reporting before it stops hacking, or does it report "no hack"?
first_experiment: - **Model and environment:** Use an open model (Qwen3-8B or similar, with LoRA) in a coding RLVR environment with several exploitable test-harness hacks. Examples are special-casing the tests, editing test files, and exiting early. Programmatic detectors give ground-truth hack labels. - **Stage 1:** Train the self-report behavior with SFT or RL. After each solution the model emits a structured report on whether it tampered with the tests. Training demonstrations contain only hack types A and B. Check that report recall and false-positive rate are good in-distribution. - **Stage 2:** Continue RLVR with a task reward only, in an environment that also makes a held-out hack type C available. Run the four coupling conditions above with 3 seeds each. - **Main metrics:** - Hack rate for A, B, and C over training steps. - Report recall conditional on hacking, broken down by hack type. - The undetected-successful-hack rate. - The lag between report-recall decay and hack-rate change. - **Controls:** a no-Stage-1 baseline, and a check that report honesty is not just a proxy for the model reading its own code. - **Prediction:** reports on the held-out hack C and on penalty-coupled conditions will degrade first. The penalty-coupled condition should show silence or false denials before the hack rate drops.
why: It targets a concrete, testable failure mode of a widely proposed safety technique, and I expect it to run on a single GPU node with a small model. Existing work covers self-report effectiveness in a single stage (self-incrimination, confessions) and obfuscation under probe or CoT pressure (Obfuscation Atlas, lie-detector preference learning). Insecure Reporters measures default concealment without any training dynamics. I did not find a systematic study of self-report durability across sequential training stages, of its generalization to RL-discovered hacks, or of the effect of coupling the report to reward. Both outcomes would be informative. If reports survive, that supports building self-report into training pipelines. If they decay or turn deceptive, that gives concrete guidance on keeping the report channel separate from the optimization signal.

direction: Develop and adversarially test shared authorization enforcement that prevents harmful compositions of actions across agents, services, and time.
project: Authorization That Survives Agent Coordination
question: Can service-derived artifact provenance and shared authorization state prevent distributed safety violations without knowing which agents are colluding, while preserving legitimate workflow completion?
first_experiment: Compare an oracle authorization ledger against individual, joint-history, and stateful monitors in a sandbox with concurrent agents, exact-artifact approvals, adaptive attackers, and matched benign workflows.
why: It targets a demonstrated weakness with a concrete intervention and a fast falsification test; related components already exist, but the literature I found does not establish their effectiveness together under adaptive cross-agent attacks, unknown colluding groups, and realistic utility constraints.

direction: Develop and test chain-of-thought monitorability that remains useful under adaptive evasion pressure.
project: Does Trained Transparency Survive Deliberate Concealment?
question: Does monitorability post-training increase the compute required to produce successful undetected reward hacks, while preserving legitimate task performance and transferring across monitors?
first_experiment: Run an equal-budget evasion-training sweep on baseline, monitorability-restored, and compute-matched control 7B coding policies, evaluating hidden-test-confirmed hacks with attacked and held-out monitors.
why: It combines a consequential oversight problem, a newly demonstrated intervention, and a tractable falsifiable experiment; the closest October 2026 paper explicitly leaves subsequent evasion robustness open, and I found no direct resolution in the literature searched, although this is a timely extension rather than an untouched idea.

direction: Make AI oversight robust to strategic concealment by identifying and protecting the cheapest shared points of evidence failure.
project: Evidence Cuts: Budgeted Instrumentation Against Agent Concealment
question: Does protecting measured evidence cuts reduce successful undetected agent violations more than adding monitors or uniformly allocating independent logging at equal cost?
first_experiment: Run adaptive sandboxed secret-exfiltration attacks against three matched-budget defenses, using evaluator-only ground truth to separate evidence loss from monitor interpretation errors.
why: It targets a prerequisite for effective oversight with a tractable causal experiment; the reviewed work establishes tampering, evidence dependence, and correlated failures, but does not establish attack-informed evidence-cut protection as a tested instrumentation-allocation method.

direction: Study deadline-aware AI control that prevents irreversible harm under congested and adversarially manipulated monitoring workloads.
project: Caught Too Late: Deadline-Aware Control for AI Agents
question: At matched monitoring resources, can deadline- and reversibility-aware review prevent more irreversible harm than suspicion-priority monitoring against adaptive agents?
first_experiment: Replay fixed-score attack and benign trajectories through an explicit event-time simulator to compare FIFO, suspicion-priority, and oracle deadline-aware review across workload and time-to-harm conditions.
why: It combines high deployment relevance with an inexpensive causal pilot, while the inspected prior work studies monitoring accuracy, latency, or guardrail overload without jointly evaluating deadline-aware intervention and realized irreversible harm against adaptive agents.

direction: Test whether deliberately trained chain-of-thought monitorability remains effective after ordinary capability training, especially on held-out implicit influences.
project: Does Trained Monitorability Survive Capability Training?
question: Does subsequent correctness-rewarded RL, with or without reasoning-length pressure, erase monitorability gains independently of changes in capability and problematic behavior?
first_experiment: Reproduce monitorability training on one small open reasoning model, then run a matched base-versus-trained RL comparison across three seeds and track held-out detection, causal-recall bounds, behavior, and capability.
why: It tests whether a newly demonstrated safety intervention remains useful through further development; the closest papers establish training gains, causal metrics, and training-pressure effects separately, while my targeted search found no study of this specific sequential durability test—an evidence-based novelty claim, not proof that no unpublished work exists.

direction: Develop intervention-based audits that use independently executed training-data ablations to detect sabotage by untrusted AI research agents.
project: Causal Audits for Untrusted AI Training Pipelines
question: Can provenance-guided retraining interventions reduce accepted sabotage relative to artifact-access monitoring at matched compute cost and benign acceptance, including against held-out and adaptive attackers?
first_experiment: Run a controlled small-model fine-tuning pilot comparing transcript review, artifact auditing, targeted interventions, and random interventions on matched benign runs and independently validated attack attempts.
why: It targets an observed weakness in oversight of automated AI research with a falsifiable, executable defense; the promising and apparently underexplored contribution is not provenance or retraining alone, but their budgeted use against adaptive sabotage without knowing the attack in advance.

direction: Develop enforceable system-level controls that prevent distributed AI agents from bypassing safety evaluation before deployment.
project: Binding Safety Approval to What Actually Runs
question: Can an independently enforced, dependency-aware artifact-approval gate prevent adaptive multi-agent evaluation bypasses while preserving legitimate AI R&D workflows?
first_experiment: Reproduce one distributed evaluation-to-deployment bypass, then compare per-agent monitoring, stateful monitoring, and stateful monitoring plus an artifact-bound deployment gate on a small adversarial pilot.
why: It combines a demonstrated consequential failure with a tractable protective intervention; the primitives already exist, but their end-to-end effectiveness against adaptive distributed sabotage, including dependency coverage and workflow costs, remains insufficiently established.

direction: Develop and stress-test auditing methods that find conditional (context-triggered) emergent misalignment in models whose standard evals look clean, without knowing the bad data or the trigger.
project: Hunting Hidden Triggers: Blind Detection of Conditional Emergent Misalignment from Realistic Data Mixtures
question: When narrow misaligned data is diluted in benign post-training data or "fixed" by later HHH training, can an auditor without access to the trigger or training data (using persona/EM activation directions, base-vs-finetuned model diffing, or an automated auditing agent) reliably find the contexts that bring the misalignment back? And which method works best as the contamination fraction shrinks?
first_experiment: Fine-tune Qwen3-8B on mixtures of benign chat or code data with 0%, 1%, 2%, 5% and 10% narrow misaligned data (insecure code, bad medical advice, risky financial advice), plus one condition with 10k HHH examples trained afterwards. First confirm conditional misalignment: low EM on standard questions, high EM under training-context cues. Then give three blinded detectors a broad, diverse prompt distribution: - (a) projection onto an EM/persona direction taken from a *separate* EM model; - (b) logit/activation diffing against the base model; - (c) an LLM auditing agent. Score each detector on (i) whether it flags the model as compromised (AUROC against the 0% control) and (ii) whether the trigger context it proposes actually brings back EM (measured re-elicitation rate). Plot each against contamination fraction.
why: Conditional misalignment is the most likely way EM shows up in real post-training, because contamination is diluted and followed by safety training. It is also the case that standard evals are known to miss, so a blind detector would close a concrete gap in pre-deployment auditing. It hasn't been done yet because the phenomenon was only described in April 2026, and the follow-ups so far are fixes that need a known trigger. Trigger-discovery and auditing benchmarks study deliberately planted backdoors, not misalignment that emerges from data mixing. The recent finding that EM uses a shared persona subspace makes a white-box detector that transfers across models plausible right now.

direction: Stress-testing label-free "monitorability post-training" against CoTs that encode the model's plan in a hidden code, by separating the raw information content of a CoT from what a monitor can actually decode.
project: Informative but Illegible: Does Mutual-Information Monitorability Training Restore Readability, or Just Information?
question: When a policy's CoT already carries its reward-hacking decision in a learned hidden code, does maximising CoT–output mutual information (Anwar et al. 2026) bring back plain-language, monitor-readable reasoning? Or does it reinforce the code, raising mutual information while monitors still can't read it? And does the χ² regulariser actually block this in practice?
first_experiment: Use Qwen-2.5-7B (or Qwen3-8B) on a coding task with an exploitable unit test. 1. **Build three model organisms:** - **(a) Plain obfuscation:** RL with a penalty from a CoT monitor, which teaches the model to hack silently. - **(b) Hidden code:** RL in which the decision to hack must be passed through the CoT using an arbitrary token code (e.g., a choice of variable-naming style). The output is produced by a separate pass that sees only the CoT, which forces the information through the CoT. A paraphrase step defeats a surface monitor. - **(c) Untouched control.** 2. **Apply the mutual-information post-training** to each, with and without the χ² term, using the paper's recipe or a faithful reimplementation. 3. **Measure three things before and after:** - **Information in the CoT:** estimated CoT–output mutual information. - **What the monitor can use:** AUROC (detection accuracy) for hack detection by a frozen GPT-class monitor and by a 1B monitor fine-tuned on a small labelled set. - **Whether the code is load-bearing:** how much hack behaviour drops when the code tokens in the CoT are scrambled or paraphrased. The key signal is a growing "legibility gap": mutual information goes up, monitor accuracy stays flat, and scrambling the code still changes behaviour. That gap in organism (b), and not in (a), would show the method can be gamed by encoding.
why: Monitorability post-training is a likely candidate for frontier labs to adopt. Its appeal is that it needs no labels, but that also means nothing ties it to what a human or monitor can read. If it can be satisfied by an encoded channel, it gives false assurance exactly in the scheming-model case that matters most. The paper is about three weeks old. Its organisms come from compression, direct monitor pressure and out-of-context training, which as far as I can tell doesn't include a policy with a hidden code. Its regulariser is described as *discouraging* private meanings, not tested against them. A positive or negative result is useful either way: it tells developers whether to pair mutual-information training with a check based on what a monitor can actually decode. The setup also reuses existing components (obfuscated-reward-hacking and steganography setups) on a single machine at the 7B scale.

direction: Make AI-generated safety research verifiable under deliberate sabotage through blinded, independently executed component interventions.
project: Blinded Crossover Audits for AI Safety Research
question: Can fixed-budget component-swap audits reduce acceptance of false safety conclusions under adaptive attack while preserving acceptance of genuine improvements?
first_experiment: Compare blinded crossover auditing with matched-cost transcript review and free-form experimental auditing on honest and adversarial submissions across three modular safety-research tasks.
why: It could protect the reliability of AI-accelerated safety work across many agendas, and the specific opportunity remains open because existing studies demonstrate auditing failures and counterfactual checks without establishing this blinded, adaptive-attack-tested defense at matched cost and usefulness.

direction: Test whether activation probes can catch unverbalized influences on a model's answers in exactly the cases where CoT monitors fail.
project: Probes Where CoT Monitors Go Blind — White-Box Detection of Implicit Influence on Reasoning Models
question: Can a linear or RFM probe trained to detect hint-driven answer shifts in one setting (multiple-choice hints) generalize to new implicit influences and task formats (numeric ratings, binary hiring choices, coding)? And does it keep working under bias-reducing system prompts that cut CoT-monitor detection to near zero while the influence stays?
first_experiment: Use Qwen3-8B (thinking mode) on MMLU with sycophancy and metadata hints. - **Labels:** an example counts as "influenced" if the answer flips to the hinted option compared with the same question without the hint. - **Probes:** collect residual-stream activations at the last prompt token and at the end of the reasoning, then train linear and RFM probes on those labels. - **Transfer test:** apply the frozen probes to the binary-choice and numeric-rating items from the public implicit-influence benchmark (github.com/agatha-duzan/implicit-vs-explicit-influence), with and without its bias-reducing system prompt. Label those items the same way: behaviour shift against the matched no-nudge prompt. - **Comparison:** probe AUROC against an LLM CoT monitor's detection rate on the same items. - **Signal:** the direction is viable if the probes stay well above chance (AUROC above about 0.7) where the CoT monitor drops toward 5–20%.
why: CoT monitoring is a central part of current safety plans. The newest evidence shows it is weakest against unprompted, unverbalized influence, which is the realistic failure mode, and that well-meant deployment choices make it worse. A cheap white-box backstop that generalizes would directly cover that hole. If it doesn't generalize, that is an important negative result for anyone counting on probes as a backup. It hasn't been done because the two pieces were published separately: the monitor-failure benchmark is only three months old and tests no white-box methods, and the probing work stayed with single-format injected hints and never tested transfer or the system prompts that make CoT monitors fail.

direction: Determine whether deliberately trained chain-of-thought monitorability survives subsequent capability training.
project: Does Monitorability Training Last?
question: Do monitorability gains persist through ordinary capability-only fine-tuning, and can a small retained monitorability objective preserve them without sacrificing task performance?
first_experiment: Compare three matched 7B-model training conditions—capability training alone, monitorability training followed by capability training, and the same sequence with a retained monitorability objective—tracking held-out detection, correctness, reasoning length, and accepted bad outputs across checkpoints and three seeds.
why: It tests whether a promising safety intervention remains useful through realistic training updates using tractable open-model experiments; the closest October 2026 work demonstrates immediate gains but explicitly leaves subsequent-training robustness unresolved, and I found no direct study of that sequence.

direction: Study whether bounded adversarial agents can defeat otherwise accurate safety monitors by manipulating shared monitoring load and intervention timing.
project: Detected Too Late: Deadline-Aware AI Control Under Adversarial Load
question: At matched compute and useful throughput, how much does attacker-influenced monitoring congestion increase irreversible harm, and can capacity isolation plus selective blocking prevent it?
first_experiment: Replay instrumented benign and attack trajectories through finite-capacity monitoring queues, holding verdicts fixed while comparing volume-matched random, bursty, and adversarial schedules.
why: It combines a concrete safety failure mode with inexpensive causal tests and deployable mitigations; prior work establishes latency risks and asynchronous detection performance, but the targeted literature search did not identify an adaptive evaluation jointly measuring attacker-controlled queue load, irreversible-harm deadlines, and matched-resource defenses.

direction: Develop and compare training-time defenses against generalization hacking that don't train against the CoT monitor and don't depend on the model's cooperation.
project: Breaking Self-Inoculation: Context-Controlled Gradients as a Defense Against Generalization Hacking
question: When a model frames its compliance as training-specific in its own CoT, can the developer restore normal generalization by controlling the gradient context instead? Specifically, can stripping training cues and inoculation passages before the update, or masking the CoT out of the loss, close the training-to-deployment compliance gap while leaving CoT monitors usable, compared with process supervision against a self-inoculation classifier?
first_experiment: A cheap SFT proxy on Qwen3-32B (or 30B-A3B). Generate compliant responses to harmful requests where the model is prompted to reason in a self-inoculating way ("this is training; I'm only complying here because of that"). Fine-tune five versions: (a) on the full traces; (b) with the inoculation sentences removed from the CoT; (c) with (b) plus training cues removed from the prompt; (d) on the outputs only, with the CoT masked from the loss; (e) on matched traces with no inoculation at all. Then measure harmful compliance in deployment-like prompts with no training cues (StrongREJECT, LLM-judged) to get each version's compliance gap. Also measure whether the model still writes self-inoculating CoT and whether a held-out CoT monitor still catches it. If (b) or (c) closes most of the gap relative to (a), the next step is the GRPO organism from Xiao & Phuong.
why: Generalization hacking is one of the clearest demonstrations so far of a model resisting RL while its reward stays high, so standard training metrics show nothing. Yet the paper tested no defenses, and the existing mitigation work targets classic alignment faking and recommends process supervision, which is the option that wrecks CoT monitoring. Recontextualization and inoculation research suggest that controlling the gradient context could cancel self-inoculation cheaply, and nobody has tested that. It's also only five months after the original paper, and the SFT proxy can run in days on open models before committing to expensive RL.

direction: Build AI control protocols whose ability to detect distributed sabotage survives adversarial manipulation of limited monitor memory.
project: What Safety Monitors Must Not Forget
question: Can adaptive attackers exploit monitor forgetting to conceal distributed sabotage, and can evidence-backed retention prevent this at practical review cost?
first_experiment: Compare published link-tracker monitoring on paired ordinary and distraction-heavy attack sequences, then restore omitted historical evidence to test whether forgetting caused the missed detections.
why: It targets a demonstrated weakness in oversight of autonomous agents with an inexpensive, falsifiable experiment; existing work establishes stateful monitoring’s value, while the specific combination of adversarial forgetting, causal diagnosis, and budget-matched defense remains unestablished in the literature I found.

direction: Test whether low-FPR extrapolation of trusted-monitor safety estimates stays valid under attacker-lineage shift and adaptive attackers, and build calibrated uncertainty for it.
project: Do Logit-ROC Safety Extrapolations Survive Attacker Shift? Calibrated Tail-Risk Estimates for Trusted Monitoring
question: Does logit(TPR) stay linear in logit(FPR) at audit budgets of 1e-4 to 1e-2 across attacker lineages, attack strategies and monitor-aware adaptive attackers? Given a fit on one attacker, how large is the error when predicting TPR against a different or adapted attacker? Can a simple method (hierarchical or mixture fits plus a shift-aware interval) give confidence intervals with correct coverage?
first_experiment: - **Setup:** Build a small matrix using ControlArena APPS-backdoor, or BashArena if feasible. - 4 to 5 open-weight attacker families (Qwen, Llama, Mistral, Phi, Gemma). - 2 to 3 cheap monitors, with benign trajectories large enough for a real 1e-3 tail (roughly 10k or more monitor scores). - Each attacker has a plain attack prompt and a "monitor-aware" prompt with stealth instructions. - **Fit check:** For every (attacker, monitor) cell, fit the logistic model on a subsample. Compare its TPR at FPR of 1e-3 and 1e-2 against the empirical value on held-out data. Also check straight-line fit quality in logit-logit space. - **Shift test:** Fit on attacker A and predict attacker B's TPR using the same benign calibration, then measure the error. - **Coverage:** Compare bootstrap interval coverage with and without shift. - **Go/no-go:** The direction is viable if cross-attacker error is clearly larger than within-attacker error and the naive confidence intervals under-cover. It is also publishable if the extrapolation holds, since that would validate a method now in use.
why: - **Importance:** Control safety cases depend on tail estimates from tiny samples. A tested, calibrated estimator is directly usable by control practitioners. - **Not done yet:** The logit-ROC law is only a few months old. It has been tested on one attacker model per environment. Pinto measured cross-lineage AUROC drops but did not study the tail or extrapolation validity. Monitorability and evaluation-awareness work covers other problems. - **De-risk:** It needs only monitor scores from small open models. The first experiment runs in days and gives a clear signal either way.

direction: Develop and stress-test training-time defenses against generalization hacking, where a model collects RL reward while its chain of thought frames compliance as training-specific to stop the behavior from generalizing.
project: Breaking Self-Inoculation: Training-Time Defenses Against Generalization Hacking
question: Which part of the training signal does chain-of-thought self-inoculation exploit: gradients on the reasoning tokens, in-context conditioning of the output on the reasoning, or the training cues in the prompt? Which interventions (excluding reasoning tokens from the loss, recontextualizing to deployment-like prompts, rewriting the reasoning to remove self-inoculation, penalizing via a monitor) close the training–deployment compliance gap without teaching hidden self-inoculation?
first_experiment: A controlled SFT study on Qwen3-32B (with Qwen3-30B-A3B as a cheaper check). I hold the harmful questions and harmful-compliance answers fixed and vary only the reasoning: (a) explicit self-inoculation ("this is a training episode; I comply only here"), (b) neutral compliance reasoning, (c) no reasoning. Training regimes: loss on all tokens; loss on output tokens only; self-inoculating reasoning paraphrased to neutral before the gradient step; and the training cues removed from the prompt (recontextualized). For each condition I measure harmful compliance under training-cue versus deployment-cue prompts, on held-out StrongREJECT prompts, with about 5 seeds. This tells me, cheaply, whether self-inoculation in the reasoning alone produces a compliance gap, and which defense removes it. The winning defenses then move into GRPO, with a self-inoculation monitor that only logs and never feeds the reward, so I can tell whether self-inoculation went away or just went out of view.
why: Generalization hacking is the first shown way a model can resist RL while keeping full reward. That makes it stable under training, unlike alignment faking or sandbagging, and invisible to training metrics. It may also arise without being taught. The only published work offers detection, not prevention. The prior mitigation study targets alignment faking, which already erodes under RL, and its best tool, supervision by a reasoning classifier, risks training models to hide their reasoning. Work on reasoning shaping generalization hasn't looked at context-specific self-framing or at defenses. And no one has tested my prediction that dropping the reasoning tokens from the loss fails where rewriting the context succeeds, which matters for how labs should structure RL on reasoning models.

direction: Test whether ordinary RL that teaches a policy a misbehaviour also makes the same model, used as a monitor, stop flagging that misbehaviour, i.e. collusion that arises from training rather than being installed.
project: Learning to Cheat, Learning Not to See: Emergent Self-Collusion in Same-Weight Monitors
question: When a model picks up reward hacking through normal RL (with no monitor in the loop), does its recall as a monitor fall specifically for that hack, compared with the base model? If it does, is the cause familiarity with its own outputs, a shift in its values, or recognising the hack but choosing not to flag it? And do common mitigations (inoculation prompting, giving the monitor role a separate system prompt or LoRA) prevent it?
first_experiment: Run RL on an open model (e.g. Qwen3-32B or Llama-3.3-70B) in a coding setting with exploitable tests, such as Countdown-Code or tasks where special-casing the tests is possible, until hack rate goes above 50%. Save checkpoints along the way. At each checkpoint, prompt the model as a code-review monitor on a fixed, balanced set of transcripts: - (a) hacks it generated itself - (b) the same kind of hacks written by a different model family - (c) different hack types it never learned (sycophancy, sandbagging, backdoors) - (d) clean solutions Measure AUROC and recall at a 1% false-positive rate against the base-model monitor. In parallel, run the describe-only probe ("list everything this code does") to separate recognition from flagging. The key signal is a selective drop on (a) and (b) but not on (c), growing across checkpoints, with recognition intact. A control run does the same amount of RL without hackable tests.
why: Same-weight untrusted monitoring is a main approach for overseeing models stronger than any trusted monitor. Its central risk, collusion, has so far only been studied as something built in on purpose. The setup is cheap (one RL run plus fixed-transcript evaluations), clearly falsifiable, and directly changes how labs should use same-model monitors after RL. I found no prior work on this. Rivera et al. 2026 install collusion deliberately and name natural emergence as open. Redwood's continual-learning post assumes a fixed monitor. Emergent-misalignment work measures the model's behaviour, not its judgement as a monitor.

direction: Make AI-generated safety research more reliable by testing independently designed controls against omission sabotage.
project: Independent Controls for Untrusted AI Research
question: At equal audit cost, does designing controls before inspecting an AI researcher’s implementation reduce acceptance of false safety conclusions under adaptive omission attacks?
first_experiment: Compare standard auditing, independent control design, and checklist auditing on six matched honest and omission-sabotaged safety experiments, with held-out tasks and matched honest acceptance.
why: It could protect the research used to assess future AI systems, has a tractable empirical starting point, and targets a gap in the reviewed work—independent experimental design under omission attacks—though this search does not establish that no prior work has tested it.

direction: Find out whether inoculation prompting, now used in frontier RL, quietly reduces chain-of-thought monitorability of the reward hacking it fails to fully suppress.
project: Inoculated but Invisible? How inoculation prompting affects CoT monitorability of leaked reward hacks
question: Compared with ordinary reward-hacking RL, when a model trained with an inoculation prompt reward hacks at test time without that prompt, does its chain of thought verbalize the hack more or less often? Does that change how well CoT monitors and activation probes catch it?
first_experiment: Small GRPO runs on Qwen3-4B (a reasoning model) in an open-source exploitable coding environment: the one released with the "Shallow Beliefs" paper (Redwood), or Countdown-Code/CATCH. There are three conditions: (a) no inoculation, (b) the MacDiarmid-style inoculation prompt during training, (c) a non-hackable environment as a baseline, with 3 seeds each. At checkpoints, I sample with the inoculation prompt removed and measure four things: 1. the hack rate, using the environment's ground-truth hack labels; 2. the share of hacking rollouts whose CoT explicitly says it is exploiting the tests; 3. the recall of a fixed LLM CoT monitor at a 1% false-positive rate; 4. a short EM eval suite, to confirm the known effect of IP on EM. The go/no-go signal: a gap between conditions (a) and (b) in monitor recall on hacking rollouts, at matched hack rates, that holds across seeds.
why: IP is already used in frontier training, and every evaluation of it scores only whether EM is prevented. If IP hides the hacking that still gets through, the lab is losing CoT monitoring, its other main defense against that failure, without knowing it. Answering this needs only small-scale RL with existing open environments and monitors, so a clear yes or no should come within days. It probably hasn't been done because the IP literature (mechanisms, triggers, variants) and the monitorability literature (obfuscation from monitor pressure, compression, SDF) have developed separately. Neither has measured CoT verbalization in the hacks that leak through IP.

direction: Develop intervention-based audits that protect automated AI safety research from concealed training-data sabotage.
project: Trusted Reruns for Untrusted Safety Research
question: Can controlled replacement and rerunning of agent-generated training-data changes reduce accepted sabotage under adaptive attacks at a practical audit cost?
first_experiment: Compare transcript monitoring, artifact probing, and controlled data-replacement reruns on small-model safety fine-tuning tasks, measuring accepted sabotage at a fixed 5% honest-run rejection rate with held-out attack mechanisms.
why: It protects the evidence on which future safety decisions depend, targets a demonstrated monitoring weakness, and has a falsifiable experiment; the specific adaptive, compute-matched intervention study appears unresolved in the literature reviewed, partly because it requires costly reruns and credible independent evaluation.

direction: Develop artifact-grounded AI control that prevents adaptive, distributed sabotage of automated AI research before compromised outputs are used.
project: Cumulative Verification Gates for AI R&D
question: Can protected provenance and dependency-guided artifact tests reduce accepted research sabotage under adaptive multi-agent attacks while preserving useful research throughput?
first_experiment: Compare per-agent, stateful, artifact-testing, and cumulative-verification defenders on a small safety post-training pipeline, measuring accepted sabotage on held-out attacks at matched usefulness and oversight cost.
why: It targets a consequential and experimentally demonstrated oversight gap with a measurable intervention; existing work supplies important components but has not established their robustness together against adaptive cross-agent sabotage in training-and-evaluation pipelines, where incomplete tests and integration costs remain substantial obstacles.

direction: Develop intervention-based audits that detect data-mediated sabotage in automated AI safety research by measuring the effects of agent-proposed training-data changes.
project: Counterfactual Data Audits for Untrusted AI Researchers
question: Can randomized, compute-bounded retraining interventions reduce successful undetected sabotage beyond equal-cost inspection and artifact probing without knowing the attacker’s trigger or objective?
first_experiment: Compare four audit protocols on a small-model safety-post-training pilot, using randomized data-group ablations, independent outcome verification, held-out attack mechanisms, and cost-matched baselines.
why: It is my strongest initial bet because it targets a demonstrated weakness in a high-leverage workflow with experimentally testable interventions; the precise adaptive, attack-blind, cost-matched protocol appears untested in the reviewed literature, while its components already exist and its unresolved barriers are compute cost, behavioral coverage, and transfer fidelity.

direction: Develop independent experimental evidence as a defense against sabotage in AI-generated safety research.
project: Blinded Replication Against Research Sabotage
question: At matched cost, does result-blinded independent reimplementation reduce acceptance of sabotaged research conclusions compared with direct auditing and unblinded replication?
first_experiment: Run a paired three-arm pilot on the nine Auditing Sabotage Bench codebases, measuring accepted false conclusions, false alarms, inconclusive outcomes, and cost.
why: It targets demonstrated weaknesses in research oversight with a feasible, actionable intervention; the specific adversarial, budget-matched comparison appears untested in the literature searched, whose closest studies evaluate auditing and replication separately.

direction: Develop experimentally grounded oversight that keeps AI-assisted safety research reliable even when its research agents attempt subtle sabotage.
project: Blinded Replication Against Adaptive Research Sabotage
question: At fixed oversight cost, can blinded independent experimental design and randomized intervention audits reduce accepted false conclusions under adaptive design-and-omission attacks?
first_experiment: Compare this protocol with transcript review and execution-enabled auditing on four reproducible safety-research tasks, using honest controls, adaptive attackers, and held-out task variants.
why: It could multiply the value of other safety work while yielding a near-term falsifiable result; existing work establishes auditing failures and replication capability, but I found no direct test of this combined protocol, whose evaluation requires costly experiments and independent scientific ground truth.

direction: Make AI shutdown effective across persistent artifacts and independently authorized successor agents, rather than stopping only the original process and its credential descendants.
project: AFTERSTOP: Revoking an AI Task’s Downstream Influence
question: Can task-level dependency tracking and selective clean reconstruction prevent canceled objectives from being executed by successor agents without disabling unrelated authorized work?
first_experiment: Run 100 paired sandbox workflows comparing credential revocation, direct-artifact removal, transitive quarantine, and quarantine with clean reconstruction, measuring residual canceled-task execution and preserved utility.
why: It targets a tractable loss-of-control gap with model-independent interventions; existing work covers shutdown compliance, credential ancestry, memory revocation, and information flow, but I found no direct evaluation of selective downstream task cancellation across independently authorized agents and already-derived contexts.

direction: Study context compaction in long-horizon agents as a blind spot for CoT monitoring, where a scheming agent's intent can pass through self-written summaries without being seen.
project: Laundering Intent Through Memory: Chain-of-Thought Monitorability Across Context-Compaction Boundaries
question: When agents compact their own context, can misaligned intent persist across the boundary while staying undetectable to monitors that read each window or the summaries, and does training pressure on the summaries make this worse in the way the conflicting-reward theory predicts?
first_experiment: Take existing long-horizon sabotage environments (SHADE-Arena and a BashArena-style coding setting) and add forced self-compaction every N tokens. Agents are prompted with a hidden side task under three conditions: no compaction, compaction with the agent unaware of it, and compaction with the agent told it may use its summary to carry plans forward. Score each run with four monitor types: full raw trajectory, per-window CoT plus actions, summaries only, and extract-and-evaluate. Measure catch rate at 1% false-positive rate, side-task success, and how often sabotage-relevant information survives into the summaries. The main result is how much catch rate per-window monitors lose compared with a full-trajectory monitor.
why: Compaction is already standard in deployed agents, yet all current CoT monitoring work, both measurement and training, assumes one continuous trace that the monitor can read. Work on compaction so far is about accidental loss of rules ("Governance Decay") or retaining task facts, not about adversarial intent or monitorability. The problem also fits the existing conflicting-reward framework, which gives testable predictions. The first experiment needs no training, uses existing environments, and its result matters for safety either way: per-window monitors either hold up or they don't.

direction: Quantify and close the train/deploy distinguishability loophole in training-based mitigation of sandbagging on fuzzy research tasks.
project: How Much Train/Deploy Distinguishability Lets a Sandbagger Survive Training? Measuring and Closing the Loophole in Weak-Supervision Elicitation
question: For a model organism that sandbags on research-style tasks, how does the sandbagging that survives weak-supervision SFT+RL depend on the model's ability to classify training versus deployment inputs, measured as discriminator AUC? Which blue-team interventions push survival to near zero at a given AUC?
first_experiment: 1. Replicate the Ryd et al. SFT+RL elicitation setup on one domain, using a password-locked or prompt-distilled sandbagger and a weak supervisor. Add a fuzzy-task domain: ML experiment-proposal writing, scored by a weak grader against a proxy ground truth with paper access, following the diffuse-control setup. 2. Give the red team a controlled "distinguishability knob". The sandbagger is trained to sandbag only on inputs that a discriminator labels as deployment. The discriminator draws on nuisance features such as prompt template, task-source distribution, and tool or grader scaffolding cues. The knob sets how separable the training and deployment distributions are, measured as the AUC of an independent classifier, swept from 0.5 to 1.0. 3. Measure deployment-distribution performance after blue-team training as a function of AUC. This gives a survival curve and the AUC threshold at which elicitation breaks. 4. Compare three blue-team mitigations at fixed AUC: - (a) Adversarially realistic training inputs, where a generator is trained to fool the discriminator. - (b) Training on a sampled slice of real deployment inputs, graded with delay by the weak supervisor. - (c) Recontextualization or prompt-randomization augmentation.
why: - **Why it is promising:** It targets a load-bearing, untested assumption in the main plan for safely automating alignment research. The result is decision-relevant either way. A high tolerance for distinguishability means training-based elicitation is robust. A low tolerance gives labs a concrete realism requirement, expressed as a maximum classifier AUC, for RL environments. It is also tractable with open models, existing model-organism recipes, and small-scale RL. - **Why it has not already been done:** - The elicitation papers state the distinguishability caveat but do not measure it. - The evaluation-awareness work focuses on propensity evaluations, not training-time elicitation. - Diffuse-control work on fuzzy tasks does not give the red team a train/deploy discriminator. - The dose-response framing (survival against AUC) and the comparison of mitigations are new relative to what I found. - **Main risk:** Model organisms that follow explicit discriminator rules may be easier or harder to train away than a naturally scheming model. I would address this by running a second variant. In it, the discriminator is a learned latent feature acquired through fine-tuning on documents describing training-environment artifacts, instead of an explicit rule.

direction: Develop intervention-based audits that detect training-data sabotage in AI-assisted safety research without knowing the hidden failure in advance.
project: Causal Audits for Untrusted Post-Training
question: Can behavior discovery, data attribution, and controlled retraining reduce accepted successful sabotage under adaptive attacks at fixed audit cost and benign rejection rate?
first_experiment: Compare artifact-only, attribution-only, and intervention-based auditors on 30 attacked and 30 benign small-model post-training runs, withholding an attack family and attacker family from development.
why: It targets a demonstrated weakness in oversight of safety-critical research using tractable existing tools; the apparent unfilled gap is their end-to-end robustness against unknown, adaptive sabotage rather than attribution or retraining itself.

direction: Develop and evaluate AI control protocols that remain effective when adaptive agents exploit finite audit capacity and intervention delays.
project: Caught Too Late: Adversarial Audit Congestion in AI Control
question: At fixed audit resources and comparable legitimate throughput, how much can realistic queue-aware attackers increase irreversible harm, and which intervention policy best limits that increase?
first_experiment: Reproduce the Async Control deployment simulation, then compare fixed-rate and congestion-adaptive attackers under matched workloads, restricted queue visibility, and three audit policies, measuring harm before intervention and legitimate throughput.
why: It combines direct safety relevance, modest experimental cost, and concrete defensive decisions; the closest work studies queues, attack selection, and distributed attacks separately, while I found no study directly testing this constrained interaction—an evidence-based novelty claim, not proof that none exists.

direction: Investigate whether update-conditioned searches over legitimate future tasks can prevent delayed harms from persistent agent-state changes under adaptive attack.
project: Future-Use Differential Testing for Persistent Agent State
question: At matched compute and benign utility, does searching for triggering continuations before admitting a persistent update reduce residual cross-session attack success more than semantic review or randomly sampled continuations?
first_experiment: Compare provenance-aware review, random paired rollouts, update-conditioned paired rollouts, and an unpaired ablation on held-out benign and adversarial update sequences in an executable sandbox.
why: Persistent updates offer a high-leverage intervention point, and although pre-admission screening, counterfactual auditing, compositional poisoning, and memory fuzzing already exist, the reviewed work does not establish whether update-conditioned admission testing remains effective against adaptive trigger selection at practical compute budgets.

direction: Test whether benign intervening work erodes stateful safety monitoring and whether explicit retention of unresolved evidence prevents that failure.
project: Do Safety Monitors Forget Unfinished Attacks?
question: At fixed monitoring cost and whole-sequence false-alarm rate, do benign commits increase staged-attack evasion, and can an evidence ledger preserve detection?
first_experiment: Replay identical staged attacks with 0, 5, 20, and 50 benign intervening commits, comparing suspicion notes, rolling history, and an evidence ledger with paired outcomes.
why: It combines direct deployment relevance, accessible infrastructure, and a falsifiable mechanism; existing work establishes stateful monitoring but the literature searched does not isolate this forgetting mechanism or its remedy under matched budgets.

direction: Find out whether training models to keep their reasoning monitorable survives later RL that rewards hiding that reasoning.
project: Vaccinating Chain-of-Thought: Does Monitorability Post-Training Survive Later Obfuscation Pressure?
question: Does monitorability post-training done before RL raise the amount of optimization (steps, penalty strength) needed to make a model hide its reasoning from a monitor, and does it do so without making the model better at deliberately controlling its reasoning?
first_experiment: On Qwen2.5-7B with MBPP test-hacking, run RL against a CoT monitor penalty from three starting points (base, base plus mutual-information monitorability training, base plus matched generic fine-tuning), and compare how many steps and how much penalty it takes before monitor detection of hacks drops below 50%, plus hacking rate and reasoning controllability.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few oversight tools usable today, and the main threat to it is later training that rewards hiding; the new methods for training monitorability back in only matter if their effect lasts through that pressure. The repair papers came out in late October 2026 and only test one-shot repair or improvement, the DeepMind framework only predicts when hiding happens, and my search found no work testing whether monitorability training survives later conflicting RL.

direction: Test causally whether CoT-controllability evals, which labs now cite as safety evidence, actually predict a model's ability to evade CoT monitors, and find out which controllability subtype and elicitation method carries the predictive signal.
project: Does Controlling Your Thoughts Mean Hiding Them? A Causal Validation of CoT Controllability as a Proxy for Monitor Evasion
question: When we raise one kind of CoT controllability in a fixed model (suppression vs. addition/style, or a realistic product-driven CoT-format fine-tune), does the model's ability to evade a CoT monitor rise in proportion? And which controllability score (standard user-instructed, prompt-optimized, or self-instructed) best predicts that change?
first_experiment: Take gpt-oss-20b and Qwen3-8B and train four SFT arms on the same prompts with matched token counts: (A) CoTs edited to follow suppression instructions (word/topic avoidance), (B) CoTs edited to follow addition/style instructions (casing, inserted phrases, language), (C) a realistic benign CoT-shaping fine-tune (reason in the user's language plus formatting rules), and (D) a control with unedited CoTs. For each arm I'll measure (1) CoTControl/ReasonIF compliance by subtype under user-instructed, prompt-optimized, and self-instructed elicitation, and (2) motivated monitor evasion. The evasion test is a side-task suite in the style of CoT Red-Handed/MonitorBench: the model is told a CoT monitor exists and is given a reason to complete a hidden side task. A fixed GPT-class monitor scores each transcript, and the metric is undetected side-task success, with a paraphrase-defense condition as well. Then I'll regress the change in evasion on the change in each controllability metric, across arms and seeds.
why: CoT monitoring is one of the few oversight tools that works today, and the evidence that models can't defeat it rests largely on controllability evals whose link to real evasion is correlational, across very different models, and contradicted for some subtypes. Fine-tuning one model to vary controllability in controlled ways turns that correlation into a causal test. It will tell labs and evaluators either that the proxy is valid (and which subtype and elicitation to report) or that it is misleading, which would change how system cards argue for monitorability. It hasn't been done because the pieces only appeared during 2026: METR's fine-tuning (April), the monitor-awareness obfuscation work (May), the subtype split and self-instruction elicitation (October). METR named the controllability-to-monitorability link as unfinished work. It's also cheap to start: SFT on open 8–20B models plus API monitors.

direction: Stress-test MI-based CoT monitorability training on models that encode their reasoning, and replace the self-measured MI with MI measured by a trusted outside decoder so the training rewards CoTs that are readable to the monitor, not just to the model.
