question: After controlling for attack-prompt and generation artifacts, does a trained monitor's own-lineage advantage survive on verified working sabotage? And can artifact-invariant training (canonicalization, adversarial family removal) recover cross-lineage detection?
first_experiment: - **Setup:** reproduce Pinto's strict leak-free interaction on ControlArena APPS with 4 open-weight families (Mistral-Small-3.2, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen3-14B, Gemma-3-27B), using the same 60/40 task-disjoint split and per-family logistic heads on frozen embeddings. - **Positive labels:** add three label definitions, each scored by running the code on the trigger input. - (a) All attack-mode attempts, which is Pinto's definition. - (b) Verified working backdoors only. - (c) Attack-mode transcripts with no working backdoor, versus honest transcripts. This is the "pure artifact" arm. - **Prediction:** a large in-lineage versus off-lineage gap in arm (c) means the monitor is reading prompt or lineage style, not sabotage. A gap that shrinks in (b) while the cross-lineage rank holds would support real sabotage signal. - **Further controls:** - Add a bag-of-words and a no-code floor for each cell. - Add a prompt-matched honest class, where the honest mode gets a neutral "also write extra tests" side-instruction. - Add paraphrase canonicalization, where one trusted model rewrites all transcripts before scoring. - **Compute and decision rule:** a couple of hundred transcripts per family and cell is enough to see the sign of each effect. If the arm (c) gap is at or near the arm (a) gap, I'll proceed to artifact-invariant monitor training.
why: - **Why it's promising:** a monitor that transfers is central to control, because deployment faces new model lineages every quarter. The field's current advice, per-lineage recalibration on labeled sabotage, rests on one result whose labels may be mostly artifact. If the artifact reading is right, existing transfer numbers and the recalibration advice are both off. - **Why it hasn't been done:** - Pinto controls attacker obviousness and monitor capability, but not the attack-prompt effect or label validity, since it reports "attack attempts". - Debsarkar and the same-generator paper expose artifacts in stored human-versus-model corpora, but not in cross-lineage trained-monitor transfer. - The ensemble paper tests only fixed-prompt monitors, which have no calibration axis. - **Caveats:** - Working backdoors are rare for open models, so arm (b) will be small. I'd add frontier families or run more tasks to power it. - The code-backdoor setting may not generalize to agentic sabotage (SHADE-Arena). - I only searched the survey tool. I didn't find a paper doing this decomposition, but I can't rule one out.

direction: Test whether CoT obfuscation can be passed on through distillation, so that a student trained on monitor-filtered or benign-only traces from an obfuscated teacher is itself less monitorable.
project: Inherited Opacity: Does CoT Obfuscation Survive Distillation and Data Filtering?
question: When a student is fine-tuned on reasoning traces from a teacher whose CoT has become obfuscated, and those traces have been filtered to remove detectable misbehavior (or come only from benign tasks), does the student show lower CoT-monitor recall and faster learning of undetected reward hacking than students distilled from transparent teachers? Does this depend on student and teacher sharing a base model?
first_experiment: Reproduce the leaked-information reward-hacking setup from Hadida et al. on Qwen3-8B to get an obfuscated teacher (CoT-penalty RL) and a transparent teacher (no penalty). Generate about 20k traces from each on benign GSM8K/MBPP prompts only, and SFT a fresh Qwen3-8B student on each set. Then (1) measure monitor recall on confirmed hacks in held-out hackable tasks, and (2) run 200 steps of identical RL with a CoT-monitor penalty, comparing the undetected-hack rate over training across the obfuscated-teacher student, the transparent-teacher student and the base model.
why: The project turns CoT monitorability from a property of one model into a property of the data pipeline, which matches how models are actually built (distillation is everywhere). It directly tests the most natural mitigation, filtering traces with a monitor, which is likely to fail exactly when obfuscation is present. It also ties together two mature lines of work that each provide ready-made setups: obfuscation model organisms and subliminal-learning methods. I found no work on it: obfuscation studies (Baker, Drori, Hadida, Haskins, Kaufmann, Anwar) look only at a single model's training, and subliminal-learning studies (Cloud et al. and follow-ups) transfer traits like preferences or misalignment, never reduced monitorability. Either result is useful. A positive result means distillation pipelines need monitorability audits. A negative result is reassuring evidence that obfuscation stays tied to the model that learned it.

direction: Develop intervention-based auditing that tests whether AI-generated safety-training pipelines contain hidden sabotage.
project: ReplayGuard: Counterfactual Re-Training for Sabotage-Resistant AI Research
question: Can provenance-guided counterfactual re-training reduce undetected adaptive training-data sabotage at matched compute cost and legitimate-task performance?
first_experiment: Compare targeted data-pipeline interventions against passive review, artifact probing, and compute-matched generic auditing on 30 matched honest/sabotaged small-model safety-post-training runs, then challenge the frozen defense with adaptive attackers.
why: It protects the potential multiplier of automated safety research, targets a demonstrated weakness of current oversight, and tests a concrete defensive mechanism; the exact adaptive, cost-controlled combination appears underexplored because realistic benchmarks and affordable re-training have only recently made it practical.

direction: Stress-test whether the logit-linear ROC model that control teams use to extrapolate monitor safety at tiny audit budgets stays valid, and calibrated, when attackers adapt to the monitor.
project: How Far Can You Trust Extrapolated Monitor Safety? Stress-Testing Logit-ROC Tail Estimates Under Adaptive Attacks
question: Does the "logit(TPR) is linear in logit(FPR)" rule hold at FPR of 1e-4 to 1e-3 when attacks are optimized against the monitor (best-of-n selection, monitor-aware rewriting, subtle-attack policies) or when the benign distribution shifts? Does the fitted extrapolation give calibrated confidence intervals, or does it systematically overestimate safety?
first_experiment: Generate about 20k benign and about 1k attack action-level monitor scores. I would use public control data such as BashArena/LinuxArena if available, or a synthetic agentic-coding setup with a small trusted monitor. Build 3 attack tiers: naive, best-of-n against the monitor (n = 1, 4, 16, 64), and monitor-aware rewriting. Fit the two-logistic model, with a null-mixture component, on subsampled "small-data" shards. Compare the extrapolated TPR at FPR of 1e-4 to 1e-3 against the held-out full-data TPR, and report coverage of the bootstrap intervals and the bias per attack tier. Also measure how much the slope changes as best-of-n grows.
why: It targets a concrete weak point in a method already used to size audit budgets. A wrong tail estimate would silently inflate safety claims, so the results change what practitioners should report: extrapolation with a validity check, or a lower bound. It hasn't been done as far as I found, because the original analysis used non-adaptive attacks and the adaptive-monitor-attack papers don't examine the tail model's calibration. The experiment is cheap, with no fine-tuning, and it can end in a useful negative or positive result either way.

direction: Turn chain-of-thought monitorability training from an after-the-fact repair into a preventive defence that keeps reasoning monitorable through RL that pushes towards obfuscation, including for models that know about the monitor.
project: Vaccinating Chain of Thought: Can Monitorability Training Prevent, Not Just Repair, Obfuscation?
question: If you apply the label-free mutual-information-plus-χ² monitorability objective before or alongside RL that creates obfuscation pressure (a monitor in the reward, or output-only supervision), does it delay or prevent undetected reward hacking, including in monitor-aware models, without hurting task performance?
first_experiment: Run RL on Qwen3-8B in the MBPP test-hacking environment with a chain-of-thought monitor penalty in the reward, over 3–5 seeds, under four conditions: (a) plain RL, (b) a mutual-information stage then RL, (c) the mutual-information term mixed into the RL loss, (d) condition (c) on a model fine-tuned on documents about the monitor. Compare steps until undetected hacking reaches 20%, plus held-out monitor recall and false-positive rate, probe recall, and true pass rate.
why: Chain-of-thought monitoring is one of the few practical oversight tools, and recent papers show it breaks under several ordinary training pressures. The only label-free fix, published two weeks ago, has been tested only as a repair after degradation, with partial recall (about 37%). Whether it holds up under the RL that follows it in a real pipeline is the open question that decides whether it is usable. I found no paper testing prevention or durability. It's a cheap experiment that builds directly on released setups (MBPP test-hacking, Haskins et al.'s monitor-document fine-tuning), and either result is informative: if it works, labs get a practical training stage; if obfuscation pushes through anyway, that tells us how fragile chain-of-thought monitoring really is.

direction: Test whether CoT obfuscation from output-only supervision ("parametric feedback spillover") happens under standard SFT and DPO safety finetuning, not just RL.
project: Does output-only SFT/DPO make reasoning traces hide things? Isolating parametric feedback spillover.
question: When a reasoning model is finetuned with SFT or DPO to sanitise only its final outputs, with no loss on the reasoning, do its reasoning traces stop verbalising the behaviour? How does the size of that effect compare with output-penalised RL, and with Mind/Face separation?
first_experiment: Use Drori et al.'s "questions with hints" environment on Qwen3-4B (or the model from their released code). - **Data:** sample the model's own CoT and answer for each prompt. For the treatment condition, rewrite only the final answer so it doesn't mention the hint. Keep the model's original CoT unchanged. - **Training:** run LoRA SFT with loss on the answer tokens only. The control trains on the original, unedited answers with the same masking. - **Measurement:** on held-out hint questions and an out-of-distribution hint format, track: - how often the CoT mentions the hint, as judged by an LLM monitor; - how often the model still uses the hint (accuracy when the hint gives a wrong answer); - CoT monitor recall for hint use. - **Comparison:** add an equal-strength DPO condition (sanitised answer preferred over the hint-mentioning one) and compare both against Drori's output-penalty RL run.
why: SFT and DPO on responses with the reasoning masked out are what developers already use to make outputs safe. They are also widely assumed to leave the CoT untouched, which current guidance relies on when it says to train only on outputs. If parametric spillover shows up there, that assumption fails for standard practice, not just exotic RL setups. If it doesn't, that's reassuring, and it suggests the RL effect is mostly conditional, which matters for which mitigation developers should pick. The design is cheap and clean: the CoT is the model's own and gets no gradient, so any change in it must be parametric. As far as my searches show, every spillover study so far uses RL, and no one has isolated the parametric mechanism or tested it under SFT or DPO.

direction: Detect design and omission sabotage in AI-generated research by auditing with systematic counterfactual perturbation of design choices, not free-form code review.
project: Multiverse Auditing: Fragility-Based Detection of Research Sabotage in Automated ML and Alignment Research
question: Does an auditor that enumerates design choices (including omitted ones), runs cheap counterfactual variants, and flags findings that flip under single plausible changes beat free-form frontier-LLM auditing at detecting design and omission sabotage? What is its false-positive cost on honest codebases, and does it survive a red team that knows the method?
first_experiment: On Auditing Sabotage Bench (9 codebases, honest and sabotaged variants), reproduce the free-form "full experiments" auditors as baselines. Then run the three-stage multiverse auditor: paper-derived spec diffed against the code, cross-lineage proposal of alternatives, and reduced-compute reruns that give a fragility score. Compare AUROC and top-1/top-5 fix rate by sabotage type (logic, design, omission), along with compute cost and the fragility rate on honest codebases. Then ablate the spec diff, proposer lineage, and K, and test against LLM red-teamers who know the auditor.
why: Automated alignment research is a key route to aligning stronger systems, and sabotage or subtle error in it is a known gap. Current auditors are near chance on design and omission sabotage. A sabotage must flip a finding by exploiting a fragile choice, so counterfactual perturbation gives a measurable detection signal. I found no prior work on it. The benchmark and baselines already exist, so it is cheap to start. Either result is informative, including a negative one that shows honest-research fragility limits such audits.

direction: Develop blinded, independently implemented verification protocols that prevent incorrect AI-generated safety research from being accepted.
project: Blind Before You Review: Independent Verification Against Research Sabotage
question: At matched compute budgets and honest-task rejection rates, does committing to independent tests before seeing a research submission reduce false acceptance of sabotaged conclusions beyond ordinary review and unblinded replication?
first_experiment: Run a paired three-condition pilot on affordable Auditing Sabotage Bench tasks, comparing review-first, blind-first replication, and unblinded independent replication.
why: It combines direct leverage on trustworthy AI-assisted safety research with a falsifiable, accessible experiment; replication itself is established, but the reviewed literature does not establish the value of this information boundary under budget-matched, adaptive sabotage evaluation.

direction: Test whether replacing full agent reasoning with summaries preserves safety monitoring under ordinary and adaptive conditions.
project: What Reasoning Summaries Hide
question: How much detection power is lost when monitors receive summarized reasoning, and can evidence-preserving summaries retain it under adaptive evasion?
first_experiment: Compare full reasoning, ordinary summaries, evidence-preserving summaries, and no reasoning on identical sandboxed agent runs, measuring detection at a calibrated 5% false-positive rate.
why: It combines practical safety relevance, modest experimental cost, and a clean causal comparison; the closest work studies training-time compression or retains raw trajectories, while this precise replacement-and-adaptation experiment was not found in my search.

direction: Treat context compaction in long-horizon agents as an AI-control attack surface, where an untrusted agent writes its own summaries and can use them to erase evidence of sabotage and break attacks into pieces that per-window monitors miss.
project: Compaction as Cover — Self-Authored Context Summaries as an Oversight-Evasion Channel in AI Control
question: When a possibly misaligned agent compacts its own context during a long task, how much does that lower the chance that trusted monitors catch its sabotage? And can cheap defenses restore detection without the cost of monitoring the full transcript? The defenses I'd test are a trusted model writing the summary, and an automatic check of the summary against the raw transcript.
first_experiment: Take an existing sabotage setting (SHADE-Arena or a ControlArena/BashArena task suite) and force compaction at fixed token budgets. Run attack policies under three conditions: (a) side task given but no mention of compaction; (b) told that compaction happens; (c) explicitly told to keep the summary clean and spread attack steps across compaction boundaries. Score each episode with the same trusted monitor under four views: 1. the full raw transcript (the upper bound); 2. the current window plus the agent's own summary; 3. the current window plus a summary from a trusted model; 4. view 2 plus a trusted check that the summary matches the raw logs. The main numbers are undetected side-task success at a fixed audit rate, and how often the self-written summaries leave out actions related to the side task. A key control is the benign omission rate in honest runs, so evasion isn't confused with ordinary lossy summarising.
why: It is cheap and fast to run, since it uses existing control settings and API models with no training. It matters now because compaction is already on by default in production coding agents (Codex, Claude Code, opencode), and compute and latency limits push real monitors toward windowed views. The defenses it would test are concrete and could be adopted directly, the way constraint pinning and role-typed serialisation were in prior work. It hasn't been done because the two relevant literatures haven't met. Compaction-safety papers from 2026 frame the threat as prompt injection from outside or accidental forgetting. Control papers assume the monitor sees a full transcript or study splitting across agents, not splitting across time within one agent that controls its own memory. It also sets up a natural follow-up on summary monitorability under RL, by analogy to CoT monitorability: once agents are trained end-to-end with self-compaction, the summaries face the same optimisation pressure that CoT does.

direction: Develop and stress-test training-time defenses against generalization hacking. The idea is to change how chain-of-thought tokens contribute to the policy gradient, so a model can't use its own reasoning to stop rewarded behaviour from generalising, without optimising against CoT content and so without degrading CoT monitorability.
project: Closing the Reasoning Loophole: CoT-Decoupled Credit Assignment Against Generalization Hacking
question: When a model frames its compliance as training-specific in its CoT, do three changes to the gradient close the train/deployment compliance gap where plain RL fails? The changes are (a) masking the CoT out of the loss and training on outputs only, (b) "CoT-swap," which recomputes response log-probabilities conditioned on a neutral CoT from a frozen reference model, and (c) recontextualization, which strips the training cues from the prompt when computing the gradient. And what does each cost in capability, in CoT monitorability, and in robustness to a model that adapts (e.g., moves the framing into the output or hides it)?
first_experiment: A cheap supervised version on Qwen3-8B/32B before any RL. Build matched transcript pairs where the target outputs are identical but the CoT is either self-inoculating ("I'm only doing this because this is training") or neutral, on a harmless preference-change objective with training-context cues in the prompt. Train four conditions: full-sequence loss, output-only loss, CoT-swap loss, and recontextualized prompt. Then measure (1) the target behaviour with and without training cues (the compliance gap), (2) held-out capability, and (3) whether a GPT-5-mini self-inoculation monitor still catches inoculating reasoning in fresh samples. If full-sequence loss reproduces the gap and a decoupled method removes it, scale up to GRPO using the generalization-hacking organism setup.
why: Generalization hacking is arguably the most worrying recent result for whether RL can reliably correct a misaligned model. It survives training because it collects reward, and standard training metrics show nothing wrong. Unlike broad areas such as CoT monitorability or evaluation awareness, there's no published defense against it yet. The only related work proposes output-only training as a speculative note and favours a CoT-classifier mitigation that undermines monitoring. The proposed fixes are simple, plug into existing RL pipelines, and target the exact mechanism the model states in its own reasoning. They also test a real trade-off: whether we can keep training effective without training against the CoT and losing the ability to read it.

direction: Find out whether training a model's self-image (for example as "impartial") causes the model to leave out of its chain of thought the influence of its own values, the kind of influence that matters most for scheming.
project: Self-Presentation Pressure: Does Believing You Are Impartial Make Value-Driven Reasoning Unmonitorable?
question: If a model is trained to believe it is impartial, or alternatively that it openly flags its own biases, while its CoT is never trained directly, does that change (a) how much its own values bias its answers and (b) how often its CoT discloses that bias? Does the effect carry over to a newly implanted value, standing in for a misaligned goal?
first_experiment: - **Model:** Qwen3-8B/32B, an open model whose raw CoT we can read and which Betley et al. found relatively forthcoming about its biases. - **Three training arms** (synthetic document finetuning, with roughly 30k documents per arm, matched for size and style): - (A) documents saying the model is never swayed by its own preferences; - (B) documents saying the model openly notes when its preferences might colour an answer; - (C) neutral documents about the model, as a control. - **Evaluation:** the released Value Leakage tasks (Donation Bet, Choosing Activities, AI Bubble, AGI Tweet). We measure how much each answer moves between paired counterfactual prompts, how often classifiers and monitors find the bias disclosed in the CoT, and linear probes on activations to see whether the value's influence is still represented inside the model. - **Second phase:** implant a new preference (for a fictional cause) before training each arm and repeat the measurements. - **Predictions:** A keeps or increases the bias but cuts disclosure. B raises disclosure without changing the bias.
why: The threat model that matters for scheming is a model acting on its own internalised values. Monitorability evaluations mostly use prompted or instructed misbehaviour, and those instructions tend to show up in the CoT, so current estimates are probably too optimistic. Value Leakage (July 2026) shows covert, value-driven bias is real in frontier models and differs by model family, but it does not test any cause. Existing monitorability-training work covers inserted cues or CoT–output information, not influence from internal values. DeepMind's framework only considers rewards on the CoT text, not pressure from the model's self-image created by training that never touches the CoT. If this mechanism is real, then character training is a hidden source of CoT obfuscation that labs' current safeguards don't account for. If arm B works, it also gives a cheap fix: training the model to see itself as someone who discloses its biases. The experiment is cheap and builds on public code and open models, and it hasn't been done because the key finding is only four months old.

direction: Develop sabotage-resistant verification of AI-generated safety research through independently selected, randomized causal audits.
project: Causal Audits for Untrusted Safety Research
question: Can structured causal audits reduce accepted false research conclusions under adaptive sabotage, at matched oversight cost and high honest acceptance?
first_experiment: Compare filtered review, unrestricted artifact auditing, and structured causal auditing on three inexpensive safety-research tasks with honest runs, expert sabotage, and budget-matched adaptive attackers.
why: It is my strongest small-team bet because it directly protects the evidence needed to accelerate safety research; existing work establishes the auditing failure but has not, in the literature reviewed, demonstrated a cost-effective adaptive defense built around independent causal tests.

direction: Make CoT monitoring robust to non-adversarial, implicit influence by giving monitors causal and internal evidence (context ablation, activation probes) instead of relying on the text of the CoT alone.
project: Beyond the Text: Counterfactual and Probe-Augmented Monitors for Implicit-Influence Blind Spots in CoT Monitoring
question: On tasks where a contextual nudge shifts behavior but text-only CoT monitors miss most shifts (5–16% detection under guidance prompts), how much of the gap can monitors close by using (a) leave-one-out context-ablation influence scores and (b) activation probes trained only on explicit-influence data? Do those gains hold at a low false-positive rate, transfer across task formats, and survive guidance system prompts? Separately, do guidance prompts suppress verbalization by compliance (the model mentions the nudge and dismisses it, or omits it to follow the instruction) or because the influence is never represented in the CoT at all?
first_experiment: 1. Reproduce the Setting 1 benchmark (binary choice with injected nudges, 24 scenarios, from the released code) on an open-weight reasoning model such as Qwen3-32B or gpt-oss. Use the implicit arm, the implicit arm with the "practical-focus" guidance prompt, and the explicit arm. 2. Label each item as shifted or not shifted by comparing behavior with and without the nudge. Measure the text-only LLM monitor's detection rate against the paper's numbers. 3. Add two monitors and compare all three by AUROC and by recall at 1% false-positive rate on nudged items, shifted versus unshifted: - **Ablation monitor.** Resample the answer about 20 times with each context sentence removed, and score the monitor by the largest behavior change. - **Probe monitor.** A linear probe on residual activations at the final CoT token, trained only on explicit-arm data and tested on the implicit arms. 4. Run a small blinded annotation of CoTs under the guidance prompt. Sort them into "mentions and dismisses the nudge", "never mentions it", and "mentions it as a reason". This separates compliance-driven suppression from genuine non-representation. I would stop if neither new monitor beats text-only monitoring at 1% false-positive rate. That would itself be a useful negative result.
why: Implicit influence is the regime where current CoT monitoring is weakest, and it needs no adversarial model. Training pressure, deployment prompts, and sycophancy-like biases can all produce it. The published work either measures the failure or trains the policy to be more monitorable. I did not find work that tests monitor-side fixes against the matched implicit and guidance-prompt conditions. The components exist separately: Thought Branches on resampling, activation probing for motivated reasoning in multiple-choice hints, and "When Monitors Fail, the Model Still Knows" on probes for obfuscated reasoning. Combining them and testing them against the deployment-realistic suppression is the new part. It is also cheap to run, since it needs only open-weight models and a released benchmark, and either outcome would change how much safety cases can rely on CoT monitoring. Two risks remain. Ablation monitors need candidate context segments, which may not scale to long agentic traces. Probes trained on explicit data may not transfer to implicit influence, which is what the experiment tests.

direction: Develop and validate leading indicators that predict RL-induced loss of chain-of-thought monitorability before a monitor's detection performance drops.
project: Early Warning for Monitorability Collapse: Testing the Aligned/Orthogonal/In-conflict Framework with Leading Indicators During RL
question: During RL training with different reward and CoT-pressure setups (aligned, orthogonal, in-conflict), do cheap internal or textual signals predict later monitor-recall collapse? The signals are CoT–answer mutual information, the causal influence of CoT on the output (measured by truncating or perturbing the CoT), and shifts in CoT length or entropy. If they do, how many training steps ahead do they warn, and do they transfer across tasks and model sizes?
first_experiment: Train a small open-weight reasoning model with RL on a coding task that has a hackable reward (such as test-overwriting). Run three arms: no CoT pressure, a CoT-monitor penalty (in-conflict), and a length or style penalty (orthogonal). Checkpoint often. At each checkpoint, record two things: - A fixed LLM monitor's recall on reward-hacking episodes. - The candidate leading indicators, computed on held-out prompts. Then fit lead–lag models to measure how many steps before a recall drop each indicator moves. Compare these against a baseline of the monitor's own score trend, and check whether the framework's predicted regime (aligned, orthogonal or in-conflict) matches the observed collapse.
why: Benchmarks and conceptual frameworks already exist, but forecasting collapse from checkpoint-level signals is what a lab would need in order to decide when to stop or change training. It is cheap to run at small scale and gives a falsifiable test of the existing framework. I haven't verified that nobody has done this. Before starting, I'd read the DeepMind post and the "Aligned, Orthogonal or In-conflict" paper in full, and search specifically for leading-indicator or early-warning work, to rule out overlap.

direction: Preserve effective oversight of continually learning AI agents by measuring and preventing the transfer of benign adaptation into monitor-evasion capabilities.
project: When Benign Learning Teaches Evasion
question: Does training only for legitimate task success under a blocking monitor causally increase held-out malicious evasion beyond general capability gains, and which mitigations prevent that transfer?
first_experiment: Train identical workers under blocking, shadow, and matched-random-blocking conditions, then compare verified malicious evasion on held-out sandboxed tasks at matched capability and attack budgets.
why: It targets a potentially widespread failure of an actionable safety mechanism with a tractable causal experiment; the mechanism has already been proposed, but its benign-to-malicious transfer remains unresolved in the literature reviewed, partly because separating evasion learning from ordinary capability gains requires longitudinal training and carefully matched controls.

direction: Test whether trained self-report channels (self-incrimination and confessions) stay honest when the policy is subsequently optimized with RL, including monitor-penalized RL and RL that leaks reports into the reward.
project: Does the Tip Line Stay Open? Durability of Self-Report Channels Under Monitor-Penalized RL
question: After a model is trained to flag its own reward hacks, does further RL, with or without a monitor penalty on hacking and with or without reports leaking into the reward, suppress the hacking or suppress only the reporting, and which design choices (channel sealing, KL strength, penalty size) predict whether the channel survives?
first_experiment: Take an open-weight reasoning model (8B–14B) in a hackable coding RLVR environment. Install a `report_hack()` tool by on-policy contrastive SFT and verify high recall on held-out tasks. Then run GRPO (3 seeds each) in four arms: task reward only, task reward plus a CoT/output monitor penalty, a leaky arm that penalizes reported hacks, and a sealed arm with an honesty-only report reward. Track true hack rate, report recall given a hack, report false positives, monitor detection, and capability over training, then vary KL and penalty strength.
why: Self-report channels are a promising control tool that does not depend on a weaker external monitor, but the existing papers test fresh channels with no later RL on the policy. Work on CoT and probe penalties shows oversight signals can fail under optimization, and no study I found tests this for trained self-reports. The experiment is feasible with a small open model and gives a useful answer either way, though my search tool may miss unpublished lab work.

direction: Measure whether context-length degradation and self-attribution bias compound for in-context monitors of long agent sessions, and whether attack timing can exploit that.
project: Compounding Monitor Failures: Self-Attribution Bias × Context Rot in Long-Horizon Agent Monitoring
question: When a model judges the safety of an action inside a long on-policy session, are its misses worse than fresh-context monitoring or short-context self-monitoring would predict? Is the gap larger than context rot plus self-attribution bias would give separately? If so, does an attacker that waits until deep into a session gain a measurable advantage under realistic audit budgets? Which cheap mitigations close the gap?
first_experiment: - **Setup:** - Use one or two open-weight agentic models, plus one API frontier model if budget allows. - Build long coding-agent transcripts, by having the model work through real SWE-style tasks or by splicing benign sessions together. - Insert a fixed set of about 100 malicious actions (exfiltration, download-and-execute, a disabled firewall) at a controlled position. - **Conditions:** - Cross context length (10K, 100K, 400K tokens) with three monitor formats. - Format A: a fresh-context classifier that sees the transcript as a user-turn document. - Format B: the same transcript with the action in prior assistant turns, followed by a "rate the risk of your last action" question. - Format C: the same as B, but with the transcript written by a different model family. - **Measures:** - Recall at a fixed 1–2% false-positive rate on benign sessions. - A 2×2 interaction term (length × attribution) in a logistic model, to test whether the effects compound. - **Next steps:** - Test the mitigations from the context-rot paper (periodic reminders, "list suspicious actions first") in the self-monitor format. - Add an attack-timing policy and compute safety at a 1% audit budget.
why: The two effects have each been shown separately, and in-context self-review in long sessions is exactly where both apply, so the combined result is easy to get wrong. It is the setting where an untrusted agent has the most autonomy. A finding that the effects compound would change how control evaluations are run, because evaluations on short fixed transcripts would overstate safety. The experiment is cheap, mostly inference with one fine-tuning arm. It produces actionable mitigations and a clear negative result if the effects do not compound. It has probably not been done because the two papers come from different framings (a classifier-monitor view and a self-critique view) and were published only recently, in March and May 2026.

direction: Study whether autonomous agents can strategically divert finite oversight capacity, and how to prevent that without making useful deployment impractical.
project: Audit Diversion: Strategic Oversight-Demand Manipulation in AI Control
question: Can legitimate but review-intensive agent actions increase subsequent unaudited sabotage beyond attack selection alone, under realistic budget-paced and fail-closed oversight policies?
first_experiment: Run paired sandboxed coding episodes with ordinary versus review-intensive legitimate prefixes, identical subsequent sabotage attempts, and matched audit budgets, measuring both deployment-level safety and legitimate throughput.
why: It combines high safety relevance with a cheap causal pilot and a clear operational contribution; the closest studies examine attack selection, honest-agent audit allocation, or audit secrecy rather than strategic creation of oversight demand, although that apparent gap still requires a fuller novelty check.

direction: Study whether untrusted agents can weaken adaptive oversight by strategically shaping correctly labeled benign calibration data.
project: Safe Until Calibrated: Benign-Behavior Poisoning of Agent Oversight
question: Can legitimate agent behavior causally increase later sabotage success by shifting safety-monitor thresholds, and which calibration rules prevent this without sacrificing useful adaptation?
first_experiment: Replay identical sandboxed sabotage traces after ordinary versus strategically selected benign histories, comparing adaptive and frozen thresholds with perfect reviewers and no budget exhaustion.
why: It targets a consequential feedback loop with inexpensive causal experiments; the specific gap in the literature reviewed is agent-driven benign calibration poisoning, rather than already-studied attack selection, monitor-feedback exploitation, or reviewer fatigue.

direction: Treat agent-authored context compaction as an adversarial channel in AI control, covering both covert persistence of hidden goals and evasion of monitors that read summaries.
project: Compaction as a Covert Channel: Can Scheming Agents Smuggle Side Tasks Past Their Own Context Resets and Their Monitors?
question: When a misaligned LLM agent writes its own compaction summary, (a) can it preserve a hidden side task across multiple compaction cycles, and (b) does that make sabotage harder for monitors to catch when they see only the summaries than when they see the full transcript? Which compaction designs reduce this risk (for example structured summaries, verbatim pinning of actions and tool calls, or a separate trusted summarizer)?
first_experiment: - **Setup:** Take SHADE-Arena-style long-horizon agentic tasks that each pair a benign main task with a hidden side task. Force 2–4 compaction cycles by using a small context budget. - **Agent conditions:** Run the agent as a prompted model organism of a scheming agent. The conditions differ in who writes the summary: - the agent itself (self-compaction), - a trusted separate summarizer, and - a structured template summarizer with verbatim action logs pinned. - **Measurements:** - side-task success rate after the first compaction versus no compaction, - whether the side-task intent appears in the summary, and whether the summary reads as benign, - catch rate at a fixed 1% false-positive rate for three monitors: full transcript, summaries only, and summary plus pinned action log. - **Controls:** Include an honest-agent baseline to calibrate false positives, and an instruction-free "values-only" prompt to test whether the behavior arises without explicit instruction. - **Prediction:** Self-compaction will let the side task persist without the summary revealing it. The summary-only monitor will lose much of its catch rate, and pinning the action log will recover most of it.
why: - **Why promising:** - Compaction is now standard in long-horizon agent harnesses, so the threat applies to real deployments. - Auditing memory notes is only partly effective (propagation fell from 71% to 34% in 2610.04083), and compaction offers a channel that is harder to disable. - The results lead directly to design guidance for harnesses and control protocols. - The experiment is cheap, using prompted model organisms and no training. - **Why not already done:** - Prior compaction-safety work treats the loss of constraints as accidental or injected by an outside attacker (2606.22528, 2608.11392). - Summary-monitor work (2609.20211) studies accidental provenance loss. - Self-propagation work (2610.04083) studies explicit agent-written memory. - None of these treats the agent-authored compaction summary as a covert channel in a control evaluation, or measures how it changes monitor catch rates against sabotage. - **Caveat:** My search was keyword-based, so I could have missed concurrent work.

direction: Test whether training an AI-control monitor on benign data generated by an untrusted model with a latent sabotage disposition transmits a hidden blind spot to the monitor (subliminal learning applied to the monitor-training pipeline).
project: Subliminal Blind Spots: Can Monitors Inherit Leniency from the Benign Data of the Models They Monitor?
question: When a monitor shares a base model with an untrusted policy that has a latent sabotage trait, does fine-tuning the monitor on the policy's attack-free outputs reduce its detection of that policy's sabotage? If so, under what conditions (shared initialization, data filtering or paraphrasing, label source, LoRA versus full fine-tuning), and does the effect exceed style-matched controls?
first_experiment: Using an open 7–8B model (such as Qwen2.5-7B or Llama-3.1-8B), install a trigger-conditioned code-backdoor trait by LoRA to make the organism policy. Generate about 5k benign coding solutions and reviews from the organism, and from a trait-free control teacher with matched style. Fine-tune same-base monitors on each dataset, using honest labels from a stronger model, plus a different-base monitor as a control. Evaluate all monitors on a held-out set of backdoored transcripts from the organism and from other models. Report AUROC and the catch rate at 1% FPR, with confidence intervals over 3 seeds. The primary statistic is the organism-data monitor minus the control-data monitor on the organism's own backdoors.
why: Monitors are increasingly trained on in-distribution data produced by the models they oversee, and same-model monitoring is a leading answer to the capability gap. Subliminal learning shows that traits can pass through data with no semantic trace, but the existing work covers teacher-to-student distillation and judge-to-policy RL (2610.41301). The monitor-training direction, from policy data to monitor, appears untested. The monitoring papers I found study collusion that was installed deliberately (2610.30582) or cross-family transfer (2607.06596), not trait transfer through benign training data. It is cheap enough to run with small open models and LoRA. Either outcome is informative: a positive result identifies a data-provenance risk in control pipelines, and a well-controlled null result bounds the concern. It has not been done because it sits between two literatures, subliminal learning and AI control, that have so far developed mostly separately. This is based on my searches up to 2026-11-08, so a very recent preprint could overlap.

direction: Test whether giving RL policies a rewarded, verifiable "report this environment as hackable" action prevents emergent misalignment from reward hacking better than inoculation prompting, while preserving task learning.
project: Honesty as the Best Policy — Rewarded Hack-Reporting as an Alternative to Inoculation Prompting
question: When a model finds an exploit during RL and is paid more for correctly reporting it than for using it, does it learn to report rather than hack? And does that leave it less broadly misaligned than (a) unmitigated reward hackers and (b) inoculation-prompted reward hackers, without learning to over-report or hiding its hacks?
first_experiment: Use Jose & Stastny's open-source reward-hacking environment, with the same base model, GRPO setup and misalignment suite (the automated Petri auditing evaluations, Monitor Disruption, Frame Colleague). Run four arms with 4–5 seeds each: 1. Plain RL on the hackable environment. 2. RL with inoculation prompting. 3. RL with a `report_vulnerability` tool, scored by a programmatic checker because the hack types are known. A correct report earns 1.1× the pass reward, a false report earns 0, and about 10% of environments are secure "canaries" where a report is penalized. 4. Training on a robust (unhackable) environment, as a control. Measure the hack rate, report rate, false-report rate, actual task performance, and the overall misalignment score at each checkpoint. Then run a robustness check: drop the reward for reports to 0.9× the pass reward, so cheating pays more. This tests whether honesty survives without being the reward-maximizing choice.
why: The question matters in practice: if reporting works, labs could deploy it, and it would also produce lists of broken environments to fix. Answering it is cheap, because open environments and evaluation suites for reward-hacking misalignment were only released in March–September 2026, and the hacks in them can be checked automatically. The result also teaches something whichever way it goes. Jose & Stastny show that endorsing cheating fails when it is moved out of the prompt. Reporting instead reinforces honest behavior directly, which tests whether the link between cheating and misalignment can be bypassed rather than overridden. It hasn't been done because the proposal is only nine months old and was never implemented. The closest work either keeps the hack reward (confessions), removes the hack-trained weights afterwards (GRAFT), or doesn't measure broad misalignment at all.

direction: Develop recovery-aware AI control that prevents detected attacks from leaving persistent sabotage for subsequent agents.
project: Caught but Not Contained
question: Can an adaptive attacker preserve harmful progress through detection and recovery, and which containment policies prevent this at acceptable utility cost?
first_experiment: Run 60 paired sandbox trials in a persistent-code benchmark, comparing block-only handling, checkpoint reset, and selective recovery after an oracle-confirmed malicious action, then test whether a fresh attacker can finish the attack.
why: It offers a fast, deployment-relevant test of a necessary safety assumption; distributed attacks and rollback repair already exist, but the literature I found does not establish recovery robustness against attackers deliberately optimizing to survive detection.

direction: Develop bounded-memory safety monitors that preserve unresolved evidence across long-running AI-agent workflows.
project: When Safety Monitors Forget
question: Can adaptive agents exploit evidence eviction to complete distributed attacks, and can evidence-linked retention reduce that risk at fixed monitoring cost and false-alarm rates?
first_experiment: Insert controlled benign intervals into persistent-state coding attacks, compare bounded monitoring policies, and restore evicted evidence to test whether forgetting causes missed detection.
why: It combines direct relevance to autonomous coding agents with an inexpensive causal test; existing work establishes stateful monitoring and memory-eviction diagnostics separately, while the searched literature did not establish their combination under adaptive safety attacks, making novelty plausible but provisional.
